title: Zillow API: Bridge Access, 5,000 Calls an Hour, No Price List
desc: Zillow data APIs run through Bridge: MLS feeds by invite, Zestimates and records by approval, 5,000 requests an hour. What they cost, and the scraper route.
keywords: zillow api, zillow api pricing, zillow api cost, bridge api zillow, zestimate api, zillow public records api, zillow scraper, apify zillow scraper
question: How do I get Zillow data through an API, and what does it cost?
cta: Need property data wired into your CRM or lead flow?
body:
Short answer. Zillow's property data APIs are invite or approval only, and they run through Bridge Interactive, the platform Zillow Group uses to distribute its data: MLS listings (invite only, and every MLS decides who gets its feed), plus Zestimates for about 100 million US properties and public records for about 148 million properties, both of which need Zillow Group's approval. Bridge says it charges no service fee for MLS feeds, though each MLS may charge its own license fee, and we found no published price for the Zillow datasets. The default limit is 5,000 requests an hour (1,000 a day for public records). Zillow's market data, such as its home value and rent indexes, is a free CSV download. Scraping Zillow.com is another route: the Zillow Search Scraper on Apify's Store costs $2.00 per 1,000 results on the $19 Starter plan, but Zillow's Terms of Use ban automated queries and scraping. We earn a commission if you buy Apify through our links.

Everything below was read on 27 November 2026 on Zillow Group's developer pages, the Bridge API documentation, Zillow's Terms of Use (updated October 28, 2025), Zillow Research's data page and Apify's Store. The daily figures and the example bill are our arithmetic on those published numbers. We made no API calls and ran no scraper jobs.

Which Zillow API answers which question

Zillow Group's developer site lists "close to 20 APIs" across agents, MLS and broker listings, mortgage, public data, rentals, transactions and Zestimates. Several are partner tools, such as the mortgage Lead Posting API and Rentals Feed Integrations. For someone who wants property data, four matter:

  • Listings for sale or rent: the MLS Listings API on Bridge. Zillow says "All data access is at the discretion of our individual MLS partners in the US and Canada" and that "The platform is currently invite only".
  • Home and rent estimates: the Zestimates API, which Zillow says returns property, rental and foreclosure Zestimates for "~100 million properties in the US". Zillow calls it a resource "really for commercial use cases by businesses".
  • Ownership, tax and sale history: the Public Records API, parcel, assessment and transaction data "going back roughly 15 years", also invite only.
  • Market trends: Zillow's research data, including the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI) and the Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI), free as CSV files; Bridge also offers an economic data API with the same metrics, by approval.

How to get access through Bridge

Every official route runs through the Bridge platform, which Bridge describes as a platform that lets "MLSs and other data providers to manage licensing, billing and data access". The path depends on the dataset:

  • MLS listings: the MLS starts it. Bridge's docs say "If you are looking to access MLS data, first contact the relevant MLS to request an invite to the platform." Bridge says that if the data provider includes data licenses in your invitation, you execute the agreements in the dashboard. An IDX feed and a VOW feed from the same MLS need two separate applications.
  • Zillow Group datasets (Public Records, Zestimates, Economic Data, Agent Reviews): register, fill in your application profile and apply per dataset. Bridge asks whether the use is personal or business, who the audience is, how the data will be used, whether it is a paid service, whether you will store data, whether you will combine Zillow data with other data, and where you are located. It asks you to "allow at least 10+ business days for us to determine your eligibility".

On price, Bridge's FAQ says it "does not charge vendors and brokerages any additional service fees when integrating with our partner MLSs. Note that MLSs may charge their own licensing fees, at their discretion." We found no dollar figure for the Zillow Group datasets anywhere in the docs, so treat them as unpriced; we could not see a price without applying. Replication and metadata endpoints are not available for those datasets, and access "requires adherence to the Zillow Data Terms of Use".

Not sure an MLS feed is worth it? For agents, the listing data is often less of a bottleneck than the follow-up: our real estate lead generation cost guide compares Zillow leads, ads and referrals.

Rate limits and what you can pull

Bridge says "There is no usage cap on the total number of API requests or concurrent requests you can make against a token. However, there is a default rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour." A burst limit of 1/15 of that applies per minute, which Bridge rounds to 334 requests a minute. Sustained for a full day, 5,000 an hour is 120,000 requests (our arithmetic). Public records are tighter: "By default, you are limited to 1,000 API requests per day." Bridge's paging example fetches 200 records at a time. High-volume apps can ask for a higher limit.

Bridge's docs note that "not all properties will have associated Zestimates", and that most economic metrics are published monthly.

What Zillow's terms allow

This is where the scraping route gets risky. Section 5 of Zillow's Terms of Use says that by using its services you agree not to "conduct automated queries (including screen and database scraping, spiders, robots, crawlers, bypassing "captcha" or similar precautions, or any other automated activity with the purpose of obtaining information from the Services)". The same section bars using the services "to develop competitive products or services".

The terms do carve out aggregate data. Information from the services may be used only "without the aid of any automated processes" and as needed for personal or Pro Use, but the aggregate figures on Zillow's local info pages "may be used for non-personal uses, e.g., real estate market analysis", and derivative works such as a graph are allowed if every page cites "Data Provided by Zillow Group". Separately, Zillow Group's real estate metrics page says its research downloads are free for public use and "Proper and clear attribution of all data to Zillow is required."

Whether scraping public pages is lawful is a separate question from whether it breaks a site's terms; see our guide on whether web scraping is legal. This is general information, not legal advice.

What a Zillow scraper costs on Apify

If you still want listing pages at volume without an MLS invite, one option is a scraper from Apify's Store. Two popular Zillow scrapers there (8.7K and 11K total users on their pages) are built by an independent developer, not by Apify or Zillow. Apify's listing for the Zillow Search Scraper says it pulls for-sale and rental listings "with no daily call limits", which is the vendor's claim. Prices read on 27 November 2026:

Platform usage is included in those per-result prices. A hypothetical month of 10,000 search results on Starter uses $20, against the $19 the plan includes, so the bill is $20; adding full details for the same 10,000 homes adds $30, for $50 in total (our arithmetic). Against that, Zillow's own research data costs nothing, and the Bridge MLS feed has no Bridge fee if an MLS approves you, though the MLS may charge its own license fee. If you weigh the terms risk and still go ahead, Apify's free plan lets you check the output before you pay.

Which route to pick

  • A brokerage, agent site or IDX vendor: ask your MLS for a Bridge invite. It is the licensed route to listing data, with no Bridge fee, though the MLS may charge its own.
  • A business that needs valuations or ownership data: apply for Zestimates or Public Records on Bridge, and budget 10+ business days for the review.
  • Market research or a pricing chart: download Zillow's research CSVs, free with attribution.
  • Listing data at volume without a license: scraping is one option, at $1.30 to $2.30 per 1,000 search results on Apify, but it goes against Zillow's terms.

Data is only the first step for a real estate or mortgage team. For mortgage teams, see our AI calling for mortgage lenders. For agents working owner lists, our guides to real estate cold calling and cold email for real estate investors cover the outreach, and our AI automation services can wire a property feed into a CRM. For other data APIs we have priced, see the Google Reviews API guide.
faqs: Does Zillow have a public API?

Not a self-serve one. Zillow's property data comes through Bridge Interactive: MLS listings are invite only and controlled by each MLS, and Zestimates and public records need Zillow Group's approval. Zillow's market data (ZHVI, ZORI) is a free CSV download.
How much does the Zillow API cost?

Bridge says it charges no service fee for MLS feeds, but each MLS may charge its own license fee. We found no published price for Zillow Group datasets such as Zestimates or public records. The research CSVs are free with attribution.
What is the Zillow API rate limit?
Bridge's default is 5,000 requests an hour, with a burst limit of 334 a minute. Public records are limited to 1,000 requests a day by default. High-volume apps can ask Bridge for more.
How long does Zillow API approval take?
For Zillow Group datasets, Bridge asks you to allow at least 10+ business days to determine eligibility. MLS feeds depend on the MLS, which has to invite you first.
Can I get Zestimates through an API?

Yes, through the Zestimates API on Bridge, covering about 100 million US properties, if Zillow Group approves your use case. Zillow says it is meant for commercial use by businesses, and Bridge's docs say not all properties have a Zestimate.

Zillow's Terms of Use (updated October 28, 2025) bar automated queries, including screen and database scraping. Scrapers sold for Zillow exist, but using them on Zillow goes against those terms. This is general information, not legal advice.
